content_voiceover: This slide breaks down the TEG tracing itself and defines its key parameters. The tracing has two phases, clot formation on the left and fibrinolysis on the right, forming that characteristic spindle shape. R, or reaction time, also called ACT, is the time from starting the test until the earliest evidence of clot formation, reflecting the enzymatic, factor driven phase, with a normal range of about five to ten minutes. K, or kinetics, measures the time from that initial clot formation until the clot reaches a fixed level of strength, reflecting fibrin polymerization, normally one to three minutes. The alpha angle measures the speed at which fibrin accumulates and cross links, essentially the slope of the curve as it widens, with a normal range of fifty three to seventy two degrees. MA, or maximum amplitude, is the widest point of the tracing and represents the ultimate clot strength, driven mainly by platelet and fibrin interaction, normally fifty to seventy millimeters. Finally, LY30 measures the percentage reduction in amplitude thirty minutes after MA is reached, capturing how much fibrinolysis is occurring, with a normal range of zero to eight percent. Together these five parameters let you localize exactly where in the clotting process a problem lies.
keypoints: R time reflects clotting factor activity, normal five to ten minutes
K time and alpha angle reflect fibrin polymerization and fibrinogen function
MA, maximum amplitude, reflects clot strength, driven largely by platelets, normal fifty to seventy millimeters
LY30 reflects fibrinolysis, normal zero to eight percent
keypoint_voiceover: Memorize these five TEG parameters and what each one reflects. R time corresponds to coagulation factor activity. K time and alpha angle both correspond to fibrin polymerization and fibrinogen. MA corresponds to clot strength, mainly from platelets. And LY30 corresponds to the degree of fibrinolysis. Knowing which parameter is abnormal tells you exactly which part of hemostasis to target.
